image_query: Shore Temple Mahabalipuram Bay of Bengal
tweets: Local legend said this temple once had six sisters, all swallowed by the sea. In 2004, the tsunami pulled the water back — and the old sailors' story suddenly looked true. 🌊

Around 700 CE, Pallava king Narasimhavarman II had granite blocks hauled to this shoreline and stacked into a temple — no caves, no carving into a hillside. It's one of the oldest structural stone temples standing in South India.

Inside are three shrines: two face Shiva, one holds a reclining Vishnu. The whole temple is angled to catch the first sunrise over the Bay of Bengal — designed by the same Pallava hands that carved Mahabalipuram's famous rock-cut rathas nearby.

For 1,300+ years it has taken monsoons, cyclones, and salt spray head-on. After the 2004 tsunami, divers surveying the seabed found traces of walls offshore — hints that Mahabalipuram's old port city really did stretch into the waves.

One temple still stands guard on the shore; the rest, legend says, sleep under the sea. UNESCO listed it a World Heritage Site in 1984 — proof enough it was never just a story. Follow @yddoseOfHistory for your daily dose of history.
